title: China Launches New Crackdown on Organized Crime
gist: Beijing's new one-year campaign against organized crime targets 'mining bullies' and 'sand bullies,' and Palmer's key insight is that China's earlier success suppressing illegal rare-earth mining since 2009 is exactly why its 2025 critical-minerals export ban on the US worked where the 2010 Japan ban failed — smuggling could not undercut it. He argues the CCP functions less as an enemy of organized crime than as a boss of bosses, and separately flags that coal has fallen below half of Chinese electricity generation while the Iran war drives a global clean-energy windfall for Chinese exporters.

themes.theme: Illegal mining suppression as export-control enforcement

insights.claim: China's crackdown on illegal rare-earth mining since 2009 shrank an illicit market that was once roughly half the size of the legal one, giving Beijing physical control over actual output.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Domestic criminal-enforcement capacity is the hidden infrastructure behind export-control power — an underappreciated component of China's leverage over critical minerals.
insights.quote: China has cracked down on illegal rare-earth mining since 2009, shrinking an illicit market that was once roughly half the size of the legal one.
insights.locator: Beijing Targets Illegal Mining, Sand Industries

insights.claim: China's 2025 critical-minerals export restrictions on the United States proved far more effective than the 2010 restrictions on Japan specifically because the ban was not undercut by smuggling this time.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: The non-obvious mechanism behind China's minerals leverage: enforcement, not reserves. Any assessment of future Chinese export controls should assess smuggling suppression, not just resource share.
insights.quote: this time, the ban was not undercut by smuggling.
insights.locator: That success helps explain why China’s restrictions

insights.claim: US defense companies searching for non-Chinese critical-minerals suppliers face cronyism, incompetence, lack of technical know-how, and munitions stocks depleted by the Iran war, meaning dependence reduction will take a long time if it succeeds at all.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Bearish on near-term Western critical-minerals independence claims; the reshoring narrative is running far ahead of physical capability.
insights.quote: a combination of cronyism, incompetence, lack of technical know-how, and munition stocks depleted by the Iran war means that the United States will take a long time to reduce this dependence, if it succeeds at all.

insights.claim: Illegal sand mining is a $200 billion to $350 billion annual global business, making it one of the largest under-covered illicit commodity markets in the world.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A commodity market of this scale operating largely off-book distorts published construction-input costs and hides real infrastructure cost bases in emerging markets.
insights.quote: Illegal sand mining is an enormous business worldwide, estimated to be worth between $200 billion and $350 billion annually.
insights.locator: “Sand bullies,” however, require a bit of explanation.

insights.claim: China's sand and gravel demand was approximately 18 billion tons in 2021 alone, the scale that makes high-quality river sand a criminally attractive resource.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Aggregate demand of this magnitude ties Chinese construction activity directly to river-basin environmental degradation — a physical constraint on future building volumes.
insights.quote: In 2021 alone, China’s sand and gravel demand was approximately 18 billion tons.
insights.locator: “Sand bullies,” however, require a bit of explanation.

insights.claim: Manufactured sand from crushed rock reportedly now accounts for 79 percent of China's sand supply, but Palmer is skeptical and suspects illicit river sand is being laundered into the market under that label.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A worked example of how Chinese official substitution statistics can mask continued reliance on the illicit source — apply the same skepticism to other reported substitution successes.
insights.quote: According to one estimate, manufactured sand now accounts for 79 percent of China’s sand supply. But I’m skeptical: It’s possible that illicit material is being laundered into the market as manufactured sand.
insights.locator: Beijing has spent years trying to bring the industry under control

insights.claim: Illegal sand mining has devastated ecosystems across the Yangtze River basin including Lake Poyang, China's largest freshwater lake, where water levels and fish stocks have plummeted.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Environmental damage at this scale is what forces Beijing's periodic enforcement waves — the ecological trigger predicts the regulatory cycle.

themes.theme: Official complicity as the real target

insights.claim: Mining and sand are targeted together because neither can operate without regulator compliance — it is impossible to hide a mine or a fleet of sand dredgers, so their existence proves official protection.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A general detection heuristic: physically unhideable illicit industries are a direct proxy measure of local regulatory capture, in China or anywhere.
insights.quote: One reason to target both industries is that neither can operate without the compliance of official regulators.
insights.locator: One reason to target both industries

insights.claim: Lin Jingquan, nicknamed the 'Sand King of the Beijiang River,' illegally mined river sand while paying off a network of officials in Foshan, Guangdong — the archetype of the protection umbrella Beijing says it is dismantling.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Concrete illustration of how criminal enterprise and local government are financially fused in Chinese resource extraction.
insights.locator: That complicity is how you end up with figures

insights.claim: These campaigns typically redistribute criminal resources rather than eliminate them, with the next generation of crime leaders simply paying off a different set of officials — often those running the crackdown.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Do not read anti-crime or anti-corruption campaigns as structural cleanups; read them as signals about which factions are gaining control of rents.
insights.quote: Still, these campaigns often end up redistributing criminal resources rather than eliminating them.
insights.locator: The latest anti-corruption campaign thus seeks

insights.claim: Palmer's central thesis is that the CCP operates less as an enemy of organized crime than as a boss of bosses, with criminal groups also useful to officials as thugs for hire and as extralegal enforcers abroad.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Reframes Chinese law-enforcement announcements as internal rent reallocation — relevant to anyone modeling the durability of Chinese regulatory crackdowns in any sector.
insights.quote: In practice, the CCP tends to operate less as an enemy of organized crime than as a boss of bosses.

insights.claim: Bo Xilai's 2012 downfall revealed that his nationally acclaimed Chongqing anti-crime drive actually involved handing protection rackets and criminal enterprises to his own cronies with police cooperation.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: The historical precedent that justifies discounting the current campaign's stated aims — the most celebrated Chinese anti-crime campaign was itself a criminal takeover.
insights.locator: The downfall of Bo Xilai in 2012

insights.claim: The new one-year special campaign follows the 2018-2021 'Special Campaign to Sweep Away Black Societies and Eliminate Evil Forces,' making these crackdowns a semiregular, cyclical feature of Chinese politics.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A roughly five-year cadence means the campaign is schedulable, not news — expect disruption to affected local industries for about twelve months.
insights.locator: China has launched a one-year “special campaign”

insights.claim: Coal now accounts for less than half of Chinese electricity generation for the first time, a structural milestone in the world's largest power system.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A hard threshold crossing in Chinese thermal coal demand — bearish for seaborne thermal coal exporters, bullish for Chinese renewables and grid buildout.
insights.quote: For the first time, coal now accounts for less than half of electricity generation.

insights.claim: The Iran war is a windfall for Chinese clean-energy companies because oil-supply fears are pushing countries to accelerate investment in alternatives.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: A direct second-order trade: geopolitical oil shocks now transmit into Chinese solar, battery and EV export demand rather than into Western energy capex.
insights.quote: The Iran war is a windfall for Chinese companies, as fears over oil supplies have pushed countries to accelerate investment in clean-energy alternatives.

insights.claim: US imports of Chinese clean-energy products are rising sharply despite federal efforts to reverse the energy transition, because demand from states, businesses and households keeps growing.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Federal policy is not the binding constraint on US clean-energy demand — sub-national and private demand is routing around it straight to Chinese suppliers.
insights.locator: Despite efforts by the U.S. government

themes.theme: Nationalist AI content and space signaling

insights.claim: Chinese nationalists are flooding social media with AI-generated videos of Chinese men beating up foreigners, mostly African or Indian, and Beijing implicitly tolerates them since some reach millions of views without censorship.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Selective non-censorship is a policy signal: Han nationalism is now aligned with Xi's national ethnic integration project, at some cost to China's global south diplomacy.

insights.claim: China plans to test forcible asteroid deflection before 2030 by slamming an unmanned vehicle into an asteroid at more than 26 times the speed of sound, five years after a comparable but smaller-payload US project in 2021.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Expect a fresh Washington panic cycle over Chinese space capability despite the US precedent — a recurring pattern that drives US space and defense appropriations.
insights.quote: The test will involve slamming an unmanned space vehicle into an asteroid at more than 26 times the speed of sound to alter its trajectory.
